Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 1:

The Surah of Fighting (al-Qital), which is also the Surah of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is Medinan according to Ibn Abbas; this was related by al-Nahhas. Al-Mawardi said: it is Medinan according to all except Ibn Abbas and Qatadah, for they said: except one verse of it, which was revealed to him after the Farewell Pilgrimage when he left Makkah and began looking at the House (the Ka'bah) while weeping in sorrow over it, so there was revealed to him ﴿And how many a city was there that was stronger in power than your city﴾ [Muhammad: 13]. Al-Tha'labi said: it is Meccan, and Ibn Hibat Allah related it from al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It has thirty-nine verses [from B-L-N]. It was also said: eight.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah, He will render their deeds void﴾ (1)

Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: they are the people of Makkah who disbelieved in the Oneness of Allah, and who barred themselves and the believers from the religion of Allah, which is Islam, by forbidding them from entering it. Al-Suddi also said this. Al-Dahhak said: "from the way of Allah" means from the House of Allah, by preventing those who intend it. The meaning of "He will render their deeds void" is that He nullified their scheming and plotting against the Prophet (ﷺ), and turned the calamity back upon them; this was said by al-Dahhak. It was also said: He nullified what they did in their disbelief by means of what they used to call noble deeds (makarim), such as maintaining ties of kinship, freeing captives, hospitality to guests, and protecting neighbours. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning those who fed (the people) at Badr, and they were twelve men: Abu Jahl; al-Harith ibn Hisham; Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah; Ubayy and Umayyah, the two sons of Khalaf; Munabbih and Nubayh, the two sons of al-Hajjaj; Abu al-Bukhturi ibn Hisham; Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad; Hakim ibn Hizam; and al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Nawfal.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: they are the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah). Muqatil said: it was revealed specifically concerning some people of Quraysh. It was also said: it is general, concerning those who disbelieved and then believed.

The meaning of "He led their deeds astray" is that He nullified them. It was also said: He led them astray from guidance by diverting them from success (tawfiq).

As for "and did righteous deeds": whoever says they are the Ansar, then it means the consolation (muwasah) with their homes and wealth. Whoever says they are from Quraysh, then it means the emigration (hijrah). Whoever says it is general, then the righteous deeds are all the actions that please Allah the Exalted.

As for "and believed in what has been sent down upon Muhammad": they did not oppose him in anything, as Sufyan al-Thawri said. It was also said: they affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he brought.

"And it is the truth from their Lord": it means that their faith is the truth from their Lord. It was also said: that is, the Qur'an is the truth from their Lord, by which He abrogated what came before it (naskh).

"He expiated their misdeeds from them": that is, what had passed of their misdeeds before faith.

"And set right their condition (bal)": that is, their affair, according to Mujahid and others. Qatadah said: their state. Ibn ʿAbbas said: their affairs. The three meanings are close, and they are interpreted as referring to setting right what concerns their worldly life. Al-Naqqash reported that the meaning is "He set right their intentions," and from this is the saying of the poet:

If you turn toward me with affection, I will turn toward you with its like,
And if you turn away, I will go off to a state of ruin.

On this interpretation, it is understood as referring to the soundness of their religion. "Al-bal" is like a verbal noun (masdar), and no verb is known from it. The Arabs do not form its plural except in poetic necessity, where they say: balat.

Al-Mubarrad said: al-bal may have another meaning in another context, meaning the heart. One says: "So-and-so does not occur to my mind (ma yakhtur fulan ʿala bali)," that is, on my heart.

Al-Jawhari said: al-bal is the ease of the soul. One says: "So-and-so is at ease of mind (rakhiyy al-bal)." Al-bal also means the condition, as one says: "What is your bal?" And their saying: "This is not from my bal," means: not of what I care about.

Al-bal also means the great whale among the fish of the sea, and it is not Arabic. Al-balah is a container for perfume, a Persian word arabicized, whose origin in Persian is pilah. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

As if upon her was a perfume-container of musk,
From between the two shoulder-blades (ad-dayatayn) there is a fragrance.

[[What is between the brackets is missing from manuscript K.]]

[[Al-lutmiyyah: an ambergris that has been dabbed with musk until its scent has spread and clung. Al-dayatayn: the hollow of the neck and the back.]]

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is because those who disbelieved followed falsehood, and that those who believed followed the truth from their Lord﴾. "That" is in the nominative position, meaning: the matter is that, or: that misguidance and guidance, whose mention preceded, have this as their cause. So the disbeliever followed falsehood, and the believer followed the truth. Falsehood (al-batil) is shirk (association of partners with God), and the truth (al-haqq) is tawhid (the oneness of God) and faith (iman). ﴿Thus does Allah set forth for mankind their parables﴾, i.e., just as this explanation was explained, Allah makes clear to people the matter of good deeds and bad deeds. The pronoun in "their parables" refers to those who disbelieved and those who believed."

**First issue: the command to strike necks and the meaning of "the disbelievers"**

This section contains four matters. The first concerns God's words: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike necks﴾. When He distinguished between the two groups, He commanded the fighting of the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The disbelievers are the polytheists, the worshippers of idols." It was also said: "Every one who opposes the religion of Islam, whether a polytheist or a People of the Book, when he is not a party to a treaty or a protected covenant." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn al-'Arabi chose this view and said: "It is the sound view, because the verse is general in its wording." "Fa-darb al-riqab" (striking the necks) is a verbal noun (masdar). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "so strike the necks, striking." He singled out the necks for mention because killing most often occurs by them. It was also said that it is in the accusative by way of al-ighra' (urging or exhortation). Abu 'Ubayda said: it is like your saying "O self, be patient!" It was also said that the implied sense is "aim at striking the necks." He said "fa-darb al-riqab" and did not say "so kill them," because the expression "striking the necks" carries a harshness and severity that the word "killing" does not carry, since it depicts killing in its most hideous form: cutting the throat, and severing the member that is the head of the body, its summit and its most prominent part.

The second issue concerns God's words: ﴿until when you have thoroughly subdued them﴾, meaning you have killed many of them. This was discussed earlier in al-Anfal, at His words: ﴿until he has subdued [the enemy] in the land﴾ (al-Anfal 8:67). ("Fa-shudda al-wathaq") means: when you have taken them captive. Al-wathaq is a noun from al-ithaq, and it can also be a verbal noun. One says: "awthaqtuhu, ithaqan and wathaqan." As for al-withaq (with a kasra), it is the name of the thing by which something is bound, like a rope. This was said by al-Qushayri. Al-Jawhari said: "awthaqahu fi al-wathaq" means he bound him, and God said: "fa-shuddu al-wathaq." Al-withaq (with a kasra on the waw) is a dialect form of the same word. He commanded binding the bonds only so that they would not escape. ("Fa-imma mannan") means either by releasing them without ransom, "wa-imma fida'an" (or by ransom). The killing is not mentioned here, being sufficed by what was mentioned earlier of killing at the beginning of the passage. "Mannan" and "fida'an" are in the accusative by implied verb. It is also read "fada" with a short vowel and an open fa', meaning: either you grant them release as a favour, or you ransom them by ransom. It was narrated from some of them that he said: "I was standing at the head of al-Hajjaj when the captives of the companions of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Ash'ath were brought to him, and they were four thousand eight hundred. About three thousand of them were killed, until a man from Kinda was brought before him and said: 'O Hajjaj, may God not reward you with good for the sunnah and generosity!' He said: 'And why is that?' He said: 'Because God the Exalted said: "So when you meet those who disbelieve, then strike necks, until when you have thoroughly subdued them, then bind the bonds; and then either release them as a favour or take ransom" concerning those who disbelieve. By God, you have neither released them as a favour nor taken ransom!' Your poet, describing his people's noble qualities, has said:
"We do not kill the captives, but we free them
when the burden of debts weighs heavy on necks."
Al-Hajjaj said: "Fie upon these corpses! Was there not among them one who could speak well like these words? Release those who remain." So on that day the remaining captives were released, and they were about two thousand, by the words of that man.

The third issue: the scholars differed in the interpretation (ta'wil) of this verse, in five views. The first: it is abrogated (mansukhah) (abrogation: naskh), and it concerns the people of idols; they may not be ransomed nor released as a favour. Its abrogating verse, in their view, is God's words: ﴿then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:5), and His words: ﴿Then if you overpower them in war, disperse those behind them﴾ (al-Anfal 8:57), and His words: ﴿and fight all the polytheists collectively﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:36), to the end of the verse. This was said by Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and many of the Kufans said it. 'Abd al-Karim al-Jawzi said: a letter was written to Abu Bakr concerning a captive who had been taken, and they reported that they were seeking him in exchange for such and such a ransom. He said: "Kill him; the killing of one polytheist is dearer to me than such and such."

The second: it concerns all disbelievers. It is abrogated according to the view of a group of scholars and people of reasoning, among them Qatadah and Mujahid. They said: when a polytheist is taken captive, it is not permissible to release him as a favour, nor to ransom him so that he is returned to the polytheists. It is not permissible among them to ransom except with a woman, since she is not killed. Its abrogating verse is: ﴿then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:5), since al-Bara'ah (Surat al-Tawbah) is the last of what was revealed by way of direct tawqif (divine stipulation). Therefore every polytheist must be killed, except those for whom evidence has established leaving them alive, such as women and children, and whoever pays the jizya (poll tax). This is the well-known position of the school of Abu Hanifa, for fear that they would return to be warriors against the Muslims. 'Abd al-Razzaq related: Ma'mar informed us from Qatadah concerning "then either release them as a favour or take ransom": he said it was abrogated by "then disperse those behind them." Mujahid said: it was abrogated by "then kill the polytheists wherever you find them" (al-Tawbah 9:5). This is also the view of al-Hakam.

The third: it is abrogating (nasikhah), said by al-Dahhak and others. al-Thawri related from Juwaybir from al-Dahhak concerning "then kill the polytheists wherever you find them" (al-Tawbah 9:5): he said it was abrogated by "then either release them as a favour or take ransom." Ibn al-Mubarak said from Ibn Jurayj from 'Ata': "then either release them as a favour or take ransom": the polytheist is not killed, but he is released as a favour and ransomed, as God the Mighty and Majestic said. Ash'ath said: al-Hasan used to dislike that a captive be killed, and he would recite: "then either release them as a favour or take ransom." Al-Hasan also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, so it is as if He said: "striking the necks until the war lays down its burdens"; then He said: "until when you have thoroughly subdued them, then bind the bonds."

It is claimed that when the captive comes into the hands of the imam, it is not permissible for him to kill him, but he has a choice among three positions: either he releases him as a favour, or he ransoms him, or he enslaves him.

The fourth: the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: there is no ransom nor taking captive except after thorough subduing (ith-khan) and killing by the sword, because of His words: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has subdued [the enemy] in the land﴾ (al-Anfal 8:67). Then, if someone is captured after that, the imam may judge by what he sees fit, whether killing or otherwise.

The fifth: the verse is muhkamah (definitive, not abrogated), and the imam is free to choose in every case. This was related by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by many scholars, among them Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan and 'Ata'. It is the school of Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu 'Ubayd and others. It is the preferred view, because the Prophet ﷺ and the rightly guided caliphs did all of this. The Prophet ﷺ killed 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith on the day of Badr by sabr (killing a captive by binding him); he ransomed the rest of the captives of Badr; he released as a favour Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi while he was a captive in his hand; he took a slave-girl from Salama ibn al-Akwa' and ransomed with her some Muslims; a group of people from Makkah descended upon him, and the Prophet ﷺ took them and released them as a favour; and he released as a favour the captives of Hawazin. All of this is established in the Sahih, and all of it has passed in al-Anfal and elsewhere (see vol. 8, p. 45 and following). al-Nahhas said: this is on the basis that the two verses are definitive and both are acted upon. It is a good view, because abrogation (naskh) only occurs due to a decisive text; when it is possible to act upon the two verses, there is no sense in saying abrogation, since it is permissible that the worship be fulfilled: when we meet those who disbelieve, we kill them; and when we take captives, it is permissible to kill, enslave, ransom or release as a favour, according to what is beneficial for the Muslims. This view is related from the people of Madinah, al-Shafi'i and Abu 'Ubayd. al-Tahawi reported it as the school of Abu Hanifa, but the well-known position of Abu Hanifa is what we have already mentioned. And success is from God, Mighty and Majestic.

**The fourth issue: God's words: ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾.** Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: this is the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It is also reported from Mujahid that the meaning is: until there is no religion but the religion of Islam, so every Jew, Christian and adherent of any other religion will become Muslim, and the sheep will be safe from the wolf. Similar was said by al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i. Al-Kisa'i said: "until the creation submits." Al-Farra' said: "until they believe and disbelief disappears." Al-Kalbi said: "until Islam prevails over all religion." Al-Hasan said: "until they worship none but God." It was also said that the meaning of "al-awzar" is weapons, so the meaning is: bind the bonds until you are secure and lay down your weapons. It was also said: the meaning is "until the war lays down," i.e., the enemies who fight lay down their burdens, which are their weapons, through defeat or through truce. The horses' armor is called awzar. Al-A'sha said:
"I prepared for war its armor:
long lances and male horses,
and of the weaving of Dawud, driven with it
behind the tribe, caravan after caravan."
[The footnote in the original: This is the reading of the verse in the sources. Its reading in the book al-A'sha'ayn is: "and of the weaving of Dawud, fully woven coats, driven with the tribe, caravan after caravan." Al-mawdunah means the woven armor. And in the poets of Christianity: "behind the traces of camels..."]

It was also said: "until the war lays down its burdens" means its loads. Al-wizr means load, and from it comes "wazir" (vizier) of the king, because he bears his burdens for him. Its loads are the weapons, because of the weight of carrying them. Ibn al-'Arabi said: al-Hasan and 'Ata' said: in the verse there is inversion: the meaning is "striking the necks until the war lays down its burdens, and when you have thoroughly subdued them, then bind the bonds, and it is not for the imam to kill the captive." It has been reported from al-Hajjaj that he handed a captive over to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar so that he might kill him, but he refused and said: "God did not command us with this," and he recited: "until when you have thoroughly subdued them, then bind the bonds." We say: the Messenger of God ﷺ said it and did it, and God's explanation of release as a favour and ransom does not prohibit anything else. God has explained the penalty of flogging for fornication, and the Prophet ﷺ explained the penalty of stoning. Perhaps Ibn 'Umar disliked that from al-Hajjaj's hand, so he excused himself with what he said. And your Lord knows best.

The Qur'an, 47:4 (part 2 of 2)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is so. And had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them﴾. "Dhalika" (that) is in the nominative position, as previously explained, meaning: the matter is that which I have mentioned and explained. It has also been said that it is in the accusative, in the sense of "do that." It is also permissible for it to be the subject (mubtada'), meaning: that is the ruling concerning the disbelievers. It is a expression that eloquent speakers use when moving from one topic to another, as in the words of God, may He be exalted: ﴿This is so. And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil return﴾ [[Verse 55 of Surah Sad.]] [Sad: 55], meaning: this is true, and I inform you that for the wrongdoers there is such-and-such.

The meaning of "la-intasara minhum" (He would have avenged Himself upon them) is: He would have destroyed them without fighting. Ibn 'Abbas said: He would have destroyed them with an army of angels.

"But that He might test some of you by means of others" means: He commanded you to fight so that He might try and examine some of you by means of others, so that He may know the strivers and the patient, as in the same surah.

"And those who are killed in the way of God" refers to the martyrs of Uhud from among the believers. "He will not waste their deeds" (fa-lan yudilla a'malahum). The reading of the majority is "qatalu" (fought), and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. Abu 'Amr and Hafs read "qutilu" (were killed), with a dammah on the qaf and a kasrah on the ta', and al-Hasan read it the same way, except that he doubled the ta' to indicate intensity (al-takthir). Al-Jahdari, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu Haywah read "qatalu," with a fathah on the qaf and the ta', without an alif, meaning those who killed the polytheists.

Qatadah said: It has been related to us that this verse was revealed on the day of Uhud, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in the mountain pass, and the wounds and killing had spread among them. The polytheists had called out: "Hubal is exalted!" and the Muslims called out: "God is higher and more majestic!" The polytheists said: "A day for a day, (in return for) Badr, and war is in turns (sijal)." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Say: No equality! Our slain are alive with their Lord, provided for, and your slain are in the Fire, being punished." The polytheists then said: "We have al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza." The Muslims said: "God is our Protector, and you have no protector."

This matter has already been mentioned in (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 234.]].

Al-Qushayri said: The reading of Abu 'Amr, "qutilu" (they were killed), is weak, because of His saying, exalted is He: "He will guide them and set right their affairs" (sayahdihim wa yusliu balahum), and one who has been killed is not described by this. Another said: the meaning is that He will guide them to Paradise, or He will guide those of them who remain, that is, He will make guidance certain for them. Ibn Ziyad said: He will guide them to the questioning of Munkar and Nakir in the grave. Abu al-Ma'ali said: Guidance may also be used to mean directing the believers to the paths of the gardens and the roads that lead to them, and among this is His saying, exalted is He, describing the mujahidin: "He will never let their deeds go astray. He will guide them" (fa-lan yudilla a'malahum. sayahdihim). And from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾[[Verse 23, Surah al-Saffat.]] [al-Saffat: 23], meaning: lead them along the way to it.

﴿وَيُدْخِلُهُمُ الْجَنَّةَ عَرَّفَهَا لَهُمْ﴾ [And He will admit them into Paradise, which He has made known to them.]

Meaning: When they enter it, it will be said to them, "Disperse [[in A, Z, L: "Draw near"]] to your dwellings." They will know their dwellings better than people of the Friday prayer know their homes when they leave for them. This is the view of Mujahid and most of the exegetes (mufassirun).

In al-Bukhari there is a report that supports this view, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The believers will be delivered from the Fire and will be held back on a bridge between Paradise and the Fire, [and retribution will be taken from some of them for the wrongs some of them did to others in the world [[addition to the text of Sahih al-Bukhari]]]. When they have been purified and cleansed, they will be permitted to enter Paradise. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, one of them will know his place in Paradise better than he knew his place in the world." [[addition to the text of Sahih al-Bukhari]]

It is also said: "He made it known to them" means He explained it to them, so that they recognized it without needing to deduce it. Al-Hasan said: Allah described Paradise to them in this world, so when they entered it they recognized it by its description.

It is also said: there is an ellipsis here, meaning He made known to them its paths, its dwellings and its houses, and the word governed was omitted.

It is also said: this making-known is by means of a guide, namely the angel assigned to the servant's deeds, who walks before him and the servant follows him until the servant reaches his dwelling, and the angel informs him of everything that has been prepared for him in Paradise. But the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri refutes this.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He made it known to them" means He made it fragrant for them with all kinds of delights. It is derived from *al-'arf*, which is a pleasant scent. A food that is *mu'arraf* is one that is perfumed. The Arabs say: "I scented the pot ('arraftu al-qidr)" when you seasoned it with salt and condiments.

A poet, addressing a man and praising him, said:

*"You have scented Kātib, whom the musk-pieces have scented."* [[al-latā'im (plural of latīmah): a piece of musk.]]

He means: as the *itb* is scented. The *itb* is the *baqīr* or *baqīrah*, a shirt with no sleeves that women wear.

It is also said: the word comes from heaping food, one part upon another because of its abundance. It is said: "silk that is *mu'arraf*," meaning one part piled upon another. It derives from *al-'urf al-mutatābi'* ("successive mane"), like the mane of a horse.

It is also said: "He made it known to them" means He granted them success in obedience until they deserved Paradise.

It is also said: He made it known to the people of heaven that it belongs to them, to display their honour in it.

It is also said: He made it known to the obedient that it belongs to them.

**The Qur'an: "O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you"** (Muhammad 47:7). That is, if you help the religion of Allah, He will help you against the disbelievers. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. This has already been discussed [[See vol. 12, p. (72)]].

Qutrub said: "If you help the Prophet of Allah, Allah will help you," and the meaning is the same.

**"And He will make your feet firm"**: that is, in battle. It was also said: upon Islam. It was also said: upon the path (al-Sirat). It was also said: the intended meaning is the strengthening of hearts through security, so "making the feet firm" is an expression for victory and support in the place of war. This meaning has already been explained in *al-Anfal* [[See vol. 7, pp. (371–377)]]. There, Allah says: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe"﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. So there He affirmed an intermediary, and here He negates it [[The text between the brackets is missing from manuscripts Z, K and L.]], as in His saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 11], and then He negated it with His saying: ﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die﴾ [al-Rum: 40], and ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [al-Mulk: 2]. Similar examples are many, and so there is no doer except Allah alone.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ may be in the nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), and it may be in the accusative (nasb) governed by a verb that is explained by "fa-ta'san lahum" (so ruin for them), as if he said: "He has caused those who disbelieve to be ruined." And "ta'san lahum" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of supplication (du'a'), said by al-Farra', like "saqyan lahu" (may he be watered) and "ra'yan lahu" (may he be pastured). It is the opposite of "la'an" (lu'a') for him. Al-A'sha said:

So ruin is more fitting for her than that I should say "la'a" (may she be lifted up)

[In al-Lisan and the Kitab of al-A'sha: "adna" (nearer) instead of "awla" (more fitting). Its first line:

With a woman of strength, a Afranah when she stumbles.

Al-lawth (with a fatha): strength. Afranah: a village.]

And in it there are ten sayings. The first: "bu'dan lahum" (distance for them), said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. The second: "huznan lahum" (grief for them), said by al-Suddi. The third: "shaqa'un lahum" (wretchedness for them), said by Ibn Zayd. The fourth: "shatman lahum min Allah" (a reproach to them from God), said by al-Hasan. The fifth: "halakan lahum" (destruction for them), said by Tha'lab. The sixth: "khaybatun lahum" (disappointment for them), said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. The seventh: "qubhan lahum" (ugliness for them), related by al-Naqqash. The eighth: "ragman lahum" (humiliation for them), also said by al-Dahhak. The ninth: "sharran lahum" (evil for them), also said by Tha'lab. The tenth: "shiqwatan lahum" (misery for them), said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

It is said that ta's (ta'as) means decline and stumbling. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-ta's is to fall on one's face, and al-naks is to fall on one's head." He said: "al-ta's is also destruction." Al-Jawhari said: "Its origin is overturning (al-kabb), which is the opposite of recovery (al-intia'sh)." One says: "ta'isa (with a fatha on the ayn) yata'su ta'san, and Allah ata'sahu (caused him to stumble)." Mujammi' ibn Hilal said:

She says, when I had separated her from her beloved: "You have been ruined as you have ruined me, O Mujammi'!"

It is said: "ta'san lifulan," meaning Allah imposes destruction upon him. Al-Qushayri said: "Some people permitted ta'isa (with a kasra on the ayn)." I say: From this is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ruined is the slave of the dinar, the dirham, the qatifah and the khamisah [the qatifah: a cover; the khamisah: a square black cloak with markings and stripes]. If he is given, he is pleased, and if he is not given, he is not pleased." Al-Bukhari recorded it. In some chains of this hadith: "He is ruined and fallen, and if he is pricked by a thorn, let there be no removing it," recorded by Ibn Majah. [His saying "shika" means he was pricked by a thorn; "fala intaqasha" means its thorn was not extracted with tweezers.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He will misguide their deeds﴾, meaning He will nullify them, because they were in obedience to Satan. The particle "fa" entered in His saying "fa-ta'san" because of the indefiniteness in "alladhina" (those who), and "wa-adalla a'malahum" came in the form of a report, following the wording of "alladhina," since it is a report in form; so the entry of "fa" follows the meaning, and "adalla" follows the wording.

That is because they disliked what Allah has sent down, so He made their deeds fruitless. (9)

That is, that misguidance and misfortune [befell them], because they "disliked what Allah sent down" of the Books and the sacred laws. "So He made their deeds fruitless" means the forms of good they had, such as maintaining the mosque, hospitality to guests, and the various kinds of acts of nearness [to Allah]. Allah does not accept deeds except from a believer. It was also said: "He made their deeds fruitless" means the worship of idols.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 10:

He (Allah) explained the states of the believer and the disbelievers as a reminder of the obligation of faith. Then He connected this with reflection, meaning: "Have they not travelled in the land of ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Lut, and others, so that they might take warning from them," "and [so] look" with their hearts "at how was" the final outcome of the disbelievers before them. "Allah destroyed them" meaning He annihilated them and uprooted them. It is said: dammara-hu tadmiran (He destroyed him with total destruction), and dammara ʿalayhi has the same meaning. Then He threatened the polytheists of Makkah, saying: "and for the disbelievers there are similar [fates]," meaning similar to this deed, namely destruction. Al-Zajjaj and al-Tabari said: the pronoun (in "amthaluha," "its") refers to the consequence, meaning: for the disbelievers among Quraysh there are the like of the consequence of the denial of the earlier nations, if they do not believe.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 11:

﴿That is because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector.﴾ (47:11)

Meaning: their walī (ally, helper) and their nāṣir (supporter).

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "That is because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe." So mawla here means the supporter (nāṣir), as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and others. [The poet] said:

"So both pudendum-like openings [of the wild ass] came to think that he [the onager] was the mawla of fear, behind it and in front of it."

Qatadah said: It was revealed on the day of Uhud, while the Prophet ﷺ was in the mountain pass, when the polytheists shouted: "A day for a day! For us is al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Say: Allah is our Protector (mawlana), and you have no protector (mawla)." This has already been mentioned [see p. 230 of this volume].

"And because the disbelievers have no protector" means: no one can support them against Allah.

Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. It has been mentioned in more than one place: "And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves [in worldly life] and eat as grazing cattle eat, and the Fire is a residence for them." They enjoy themselves in this world like cattle, having no concern except their bellies and their private parts, heedless of what lies ahead of them. It was also said: the believer in this world takes provision, the hypocrite adorns himself, and the disbeliever enjoys himself. "And the Fire is a residence for them" means a place of abode and a dwelling.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how many a town﴾. The discussion of "ka'ayyin" has already passed in (Al 'Imran) [see vol. 4, p. 228]. Here it carries the meaning of "kam" (how many), i.e., "and how many a town." Al-Akhfash cited the verse of Labid:

"And how many kings and common folk have we seen, and the key of a fetter for the shackled prisoner."

So its meaning is: "and how many a people of a town."

﴿It is mightier in strength than your town which has expelled you﴾, i.e., its people expelled you. ﴿So there is no helper for them.﴾ Qatadah and Ibn 'Abbas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) went out of Makkah to the cave, he turned toward Makkah and said: [O Allah, you are the dearest of lands to Allah, and you are the dearest of lands to me. Had the polytheists not expelled me from you, I would not have left you.] Then the verse was revealed. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it, and it is a sound hadith.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾ The alif is an alif of affirmation (taqrir). The meaning of "upon clear evidence" is upon firmness and certainty, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Abu al-'Aliyah said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). And "al-bayyinah" is the revelation (al-wahy). ﴿Like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive﴾, that is, the worship of idols, and this is Abu Jahl and the disbelievers.

﴿And they follow their desires﴾, that is, what they desire. This beautification is from Allah in terms of creation (khalqan). It is permissible that it is from Satan, as invitation and whispering (waswasah). It is also permissible that it is from the disbeliever himself, meaning he beautified for himself the evil of his deeds and persisted in disbelief. He said "evil" (su'u) according to the wording of "man" (min), and "they followed" according to its meaning.

**Allah's words, ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾.** When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens﴾ [al-Hajj: 14], He described those gardens, meaning the attributes of the Garden prepared for the God-fearing. The discussion of this has already passed in "al-Ra'd" [[See vol. 9, p. (324)]]. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib recited it as, "Mithāl al-Janna allatī wuʿida al-muttaqūn" (the *mithāl*, or description, of the Garden...).

**﴿Therein are rivers of water unaltered﴾**, meaning not changed in smell. *Āsin* is like *ājin* (both mean stagnant or foul-smelling). Water has *asana* (*yaʾsinu*/*yaʾsunu*, "to become foul") and *ajana* (*yaʾjunu*/*yaʾjinu*, "to become foul") with the verbal noun *asnan* and *ujūnan* respectively, when its smell changes. It may also be pronounced with a kasra in both: *ajina* and *asina*, *yaʾsanu* and *yaʾjanu*, with the verbal nouns *asnan* and *ajnan*, as stated by al-Yazīdī. Also, *asina al-rajul* (with a kasra in the past tense only, and no other vowel) means a man who enters a well and is struck by a foul odour from the well or something else, so that he faints or his head spins. Zuhayr said:

*"I will leave the warrior yellowed at his fingertips,*
*swaying on the spear like the swaying of a water-drawer who has been overcome by the stench."*

It is also narrated as *al-wasin*. *Ta'assana al-mā'* means the water changed. Abū Zayd said: *ta'assana ʿalayya ta'assunan* means he fell ill and was slow (in coming to me). Abū ʿAmr said: *ta'assana al-rajul abāhu* means he took on his father's character. Al-Liḥyānī said: it means he resembled him in appearance. The common reading is *āsin* with a long vowel (*mad*). Ibn Kathīr and Ḥumayd read *asin* with a short vowel; both are dialectal forms, like *ḥādhir* and *ḥadhir*. Al-Akhfash said: *asin* (the past form) refers to the present state, while *āsin* (on the pattern of the active participle, *fāʿil*) refers to the future.

**﴿And rivers of milk, its taste unchanged﴾**, meaning it does not turn sour through long standing, as the milk of this world turns to sourness.

**﴿And rivers of wine, a delight to the drinkers﴾**, meaning feet do not soil it and hands do not cloud it, as with the wine of this world. It is pleasant in taste and good to drink, and drinkers do not dislike it. It is said: *sharāb ladhdh* and *ladhīdh* have the same meaning, and *istaladhdhahu* means he considered it delicious.

**﴿And rivers of honey, clarified﴾**. *ʿAsal* is what flows from the saliva of bees. *Muṣaffā* means cleared of wax and impurities. Allah created it in this state; it was not cooked on fire, nor did the bees soil it.

In al-Tirmidhī, from Ḥakīm ibn Muʿāwiya, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "In the Garden there is a sea of water, a sea of honey, a sea of milk, and a sea of wine, and then the rivers branch out from them." He (al-Tirmidhī) said: this is a *ḥadīth ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ* (a good, sound hadith).

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sayḥān, Jayḥān, the Nile and the Euphrates are all rivers of the Garden." Kaʿb said: The River Tigris is the river of the water of the people of the Garden, the River Euphrates is the river of their milk, the River of Egypt is the river of their wine, and the River Sayḥān is the river of their honey. These four rivers flow out from the River al-Kawthar.

*ʿAsal* is masculine and feminine.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: "*min ʿasalin muṣaffā*" means it did not come out of the bellies of bees.

**﴿And for them therein is of every fruit﴾**: *min* here is additional, for emphasis.

**﴿And forgiveness from their Lord﴾**, meaning for their sins.

**﴿Like one who abides forever in the Fire?﴾** Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning is, "Is one who abides forever in this bliss like one who abides forever in the Fire?" Al-Zajjāj said: meaning, "Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord and is given these things like one whose evil deeds are made attractive to him, while he abides forever in the Fire?" So His saying *"kaman"* (like one) is a substitute (*badal*) for His saying ﴿Is one whose evil deed is made attractive to him﴾ [Fāṭir: 8].

Ibn Kaysān said: the likeness of this Garden, in which are fruits and rivers, is like the likeness of the Fire in which are boiling water and *zaqqūm*. And the likeness of the people of the Garden in everlasting bliss is like the likeness of the people of the Fire in lasting punishment.

**﴿And they are given to drink boiling water﴾**, meaning hot, extremely boiling. When it comes near them it scorches their faces and the skin of their heads falls off. When they drink it, it cuts their intestines and brings them out from their posteriors. *Al-amʿāʾ* is the plural of *miʿan*; the dual is *miʿayān*, and it is the whole of what is in the belly of the intestines.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verses 16–17:

Allah's words: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ — that is, among those who enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat. And "their evil deeds were made attractive to them" — a people who listen to you, and they are the hypocrites: ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifa'a ibn al-Tabut, Zayd ibn al-Suhayt [[Thus in the originals. In the Sira of Ibn Hisham and Ibn al-Athir (Europe edition), it is "al-Sulayt" with a taʾ above. In Tarikh al-Tabari (Europe edition, first part, p. 1699), it is "al-Lusayb" with a bāʾ below.]] al-Harith ibn ʿAmr, and Malik ibn Dukhshum. They used to attend the Friday sermon, and when they heard mention of the hypocrites in it, they turned away from it, and when they went out they asked about it. This was related by al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

It is also said: they used to attend the Messenger of Allah ﷺ together with the believers, listening to what he said; the believer would retain it, while the disbeliever would not.

"Until, when they went out from your presence" — that is, when they left your assembly.

"They say to those who have been given knowledge" — ʿIkrimah said: this is ʿAbd Allah ibn al-ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAbbas said: I was among those who were asked, meaning I was among those who had been given knowledge. In a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas: he means ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud. Likewise ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah said: it is ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud. al-Qasim ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman said: it is Abu al-Darda'. Ibn Zayd said: they are the Companions.

The poet said [[It is al-Hutay'a.]]:

"And the secret of their neighbour is forbidden to them, and their neighbour eats the first of the dishes."

Another said [[It is Luqayt ibn Zurarah. al-Nashil is meat cooked without seasoning. al-Rughf is the plural of raghif. It is said: arghifah and raghfan.]]:

"Indeed roast meat, and nashil, and rughf, and the beautiful singing-girl, and the first cup,
for those who thrust with spears, while the horses are sluggish."

[[In the originals: "hanaf," and the correction is from Lisan, root "qatf." This verse appears in Lisan, root "nashl," as "lil-dharibin al-hama wa-al-khayl qatf." Qatafat al-dabbah means the animal went badly and slowed down.]]

And Imru' al-Qays said:

"He has set off, carrying me at its nose [[Its completion: 'not tightly girthed, its flank well-tied.']]"

meaning at its beginning. The "anf" of everything is its beginning.

Qatadah said concerning these hypocrites: people are of two kinds: a man who understood from Allah and benefited from what he heard, and a man who did not understand and did not benefit from what he heard. It was said: people are of three kinds: a listener who acts, a listener who understands, and a listener who is heedless and abandons.

Allah's words: ﴿These are those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾ — so they did not believe. "And they followed their desires" — in disbelief. "And as for those who are guided" — that is, to faith, Allah increases them in guidance. It is also said: the Prophet ﷺ increased them in guidance. It is also said: what they hear of the Quran is guidance, meaning their certainty is multiplied. al-Farra' said: the hypocrites' turning away and mockery increased them in guidance. It is also said: the descent of the abrogating ruling increased them in guidance.

Regarding the guidance that increased them, there are four opinions: first, it increased them in knowledge, said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Second, they knew what they heard and acted on what they knew, said by al-Dahhak. Third, it increased them in insight into their religion and confirmation of their Prophet, said by al-Kalbi. Fourth, it expanded their hearts with the faith they held.

"And He gave them their taqwa" — that is, He inspired them with it. It is also said there are five aspects: first, He gave them fear (of Allah), said by al-Rabi'. Second, the reward of their taqwa in the Hereafter, said by al-Suddi. Third, He enabled them to do the deed that was obligatory upon them, said by Muqatil. Fourth, He made clear to them what to guard against, said by Ibn Ziyad and also al-Suddi. Fifth, it is the abandonment of the abrogated and acting upon the abrogating, said by ʿAtiyyah. al-Mawardi: and it is possible. Sixth: it is the abandonment of concessions and the taking up of the firm obligations.

It is also recited as "wa-aʿtahum" instead of "wa-atahum." ʿIkrimah said: this was revealed concerning those among the People of the Book who believed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do they await only the Hour, that it come upon them suddenly?﴾ That is, unexpectedly (fajʼatan). This is a warning to the disbelievers. ﴿Its portents have already come﴾, that is, its signs (amarat) and indications (ʻalamat). They had read in their books that Muhammad ﷺ is the last of the prophets, so his being sent is one of its portents and proofs. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Hasan. In the Sahih, on the authority of Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and he joined the index and middle fingers. This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also narrated it. It is also related with the wording: "I was sent while the Hour is like the two horses of a race."

It has been said: the portents of the Hour (ashrat al-sa'ah) are its causes which are less than its major events. From this comes the saying for the lowly among people: al-shurat (the lowly ones). It has also been said that the signs of the Hour mean the splitting of the moon and the smoke, as al-Hasan also said. From al-Kalbi: the abundance of wealth and trade, false testimony, severing of ties of kinship, the scarcity of the noble and the abundance of the base. We have dealt with this subject fully in our book "al-Tadhkirah," and all praise is due to Allah.

The singular of ashrat is sharat, and its origin is "markers" (al-a'lam). From it comes the word al-shurat (police), because they set for themselves a sign by which they are recognized. From it also comes the stipulation (al-shart) in sale and other contracts. Abu al-Aswad said:

"If you have indeed resolved to cut off between us, then you have already set the portents of its beginning to appear."

It is said: Fulan ashrata nafsahu fi 'amal kadha, meaning he made himself aware of it and designated it for himself. Aws ibn Hajar, describing a man who lowered himself by a rope from the top of a mountain to a nab'ah [the nab'ah (singular of nab'): a tree of the mountains from which bows are made], cutting it to make a bow from it, said:

"So he designated himself for it while he was gripping, and he cast his ropes and trust."

﴿that it come upon them suddenly﴾: "an" (that) is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "al-sa'ah" (the Hour), like His saying "an tatauhum" from His saying: ﴿men believers and women believers﴾ [verse 25 of surah al-Fath]. It is also read as "baghtatan" on the pattern of "jarbatan" [al-jarbah (with fatha and shadda): a herd of wild asses; it may also be said of strong people when they are a group of equals: jarbah], and it is a rare form not found in its counterparts in the sources, and it is transmitted from Abu 'Amr. Al-Zamakhshari said: How I fear that it is an error by the narrator from Abu 'Amr, and that the correct reading is "baghtatan" with a fatha on the ghayn without shadda, like the reading of al-Hasan. It is also transmitted from Abu Ja'far al-Rawwas and others of the people of Makkah: "in tatihim baghtatan" (if it comes upon them suddenly). Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "in tatihim baghtatan" stops on "al-sa'ah" and then begins the conditional clause anew. Whatever doubt the statement may contain is referred back to the creatures, as if He said: if they doubt its coming, then "its portents have already come."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So how will they have their reminder when it has come to them?﴾ "Dhikrahum" is the subject (mubtada') and "fa-anna lahum" is the predicate (khabar). The pronoun in "jaa'atbum" refers to the Hour; the meaning is: from where will they have remembrance when the Hour has come to them? This was said by Qatadah and others. It has also been said: how will they have salvation when the reminder comes to them at the coming of the Hour? This was said by Ibn Zayd. Regarding "al-dhikra" there are two views: first, their being reminded of what good or evil they did. Second, it is their being called by their names, as good tidings and as warning. Aban related from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Make your names good, for you will be called by them on the Day of Resurrection: 'O so-and-so, arise to your light; O so-and-so, arise, there is no light for you.'" [Mentioned by al-Mawardi.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾. Al-Mawardi said: In it, although the Messenger was knowing of Allah, there are three aspects. The first: meaning, "Know that Allah has made you know that there is no deity except Allah." The second: what you have known through reasoning (istidlal), know it as a certain report. The third: meaning, "Remember that there is no deity except Allah," so remembrance is expressed by knowledge because it arises from it.

It is related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that he was asked about the virtue of knowledge, and he said: "Have you not heard His saying when He began with it: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾? So He commanded action after knowledge." And He said: ﴿Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement... to His saying... race toward forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [al-Hadid: 20-21]. And He said: "And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial" [al-Anfal: 28]. Then He said afterward: ﴿So beware of them﴾ [at-Taghabun: 14], in His saying, exalted is He: "O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them" (verse 14, surah at-Taghabun). And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, indeed, for Allah is one fifth of it﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. Then He commanded action afterward.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ may bear two meanings. One: meaning, "Ask Allah's forgiveness that a sin should occur from you." The second: "Ask Allah's forgiveness so that He may protect you from sins." It was also said: when He mentioned to him the condition of the disbelievers and the believers, He commanded him to remain firm in faith, i.e., "Remain upon what you are upon of monotheism, sincerity, and caution against what would require seeking forgiveness." It was also said: the address is to him, but what is meant is the Ummah, and according to this view the verse makes it obligatory for a person to seek forgiveness for all Muslims. It was also said: the Prophet, peace be upon him, would feel constriction in his chest because of the disbelief of the disbelievers and the hypocrites, so the verse was revealed, meaning: "Know that there is no remover who removes what is upon you except Allah, so do not attach your heart to anyone besides Him." It was also said: he was commanded to seek forgiveness so that the Ummah would follow him. ﴿And for the believing men and believing women﴾, i.e., and for their sins. This is a command to intercession.

Muslim related from 'Asim al-Ahwal, from Abdullah ibn Sarjis al-Makhzumi, who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and I ate from his food. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, may Allah forgive you!" My companion said to him: "Did the Prophet (ﷺ) ask forgiveness for you?" He said: "Yes, and for you." Then he recited this verse: "And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women." Then I turned around and looked at the seal of prophethood between his shoulders, gathered [like a fist, meaning the fingers were gathered and pressed together] [upon it [an addition from Sahih Muslim. Al-khaylan: plural of khal, a mole on the body. Ath-tha'alil: plural of tha'lul, small bumps rising on the body]] like moles, as if they were warts.

﴿And Allah knows your moving about and your resting place﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions. The first: He knows your deeds in your movement and your residence. The second: "your moving about" in your deeds by day, "and your resting place" in your nights, asleep. It was also said: "your moving about" in this world, "and your resting place" in this world and the Hereafter; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. 'Ikrimah said: "your moving about" is through the loins of fathers to the wombs of mothers, and "your resting place" is your dwelling on the earth. Ibn Kaysan said: "your moving about" is from back to belly, to this world, and "your resting place" is in the graves.

I say: The generality encompasses all of this, so nothing of the movements and stillnesses of the children of Adam is hidden from Him, exalted is He, and likewise all His creation. He knows all of that before its existence, in totality and in detail, first and last. Glory be to Him! There is no deity except Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 20–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who believe say﴾, i.e., the sincere believers. "Why has a surah not been sent down?" out of longing for revelation and eagerness for jihad and its reward. The meaning of "lawla" (why not, if only) is "halla" (why not). "But when a decisive surah is sent down" in which there is no abrogation (naskh). Qatadah said: every surah in which jihad is mentioned is muhkamah (decisive), and it is the hardest of the Qur'an upon the hypocrites. In the recitation of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "fa-idha unzilat surah muhdathah" (a newly revealed surah), meaning newly revealed. "And fighting is mentioned in it" i.e., jihad was made obligatory in it. It was also read "fa-idha unzilat surah wa dhukira fihā al-qitāl" with the verb in the active form and "al-qitāl" in the accusative. "You see those in whose hearts is a disease" i.e., doubt and hypocrisy, "looking at you with the look of one who has fainted from death" i.e., the look of those overcome and enraged, with a fixed and staring gaze, like one whose eyes become fixed at the time of death; this is because of their cowardice toward fighting, out of fear and panic, and because of their secret inclination toward the disbelievers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Obedience and fair speech would be better for them﴾. "Fa-awla lahum" (woe to them / nearer to ruin for them). Al-Jawhari said: the saying "awla laka" is a threat and a warning. The poet said:

Fa-awla thumma awla thumma awla... wa-hal lil-darr yuhlabu min maradd

Al-Asma'i said: its meaning is that what would destroy him has come near to him, i.e., has descended upon him. He recited:

Fa-'adda bayna hadiyatayni minha... wa-awla an yazid 'ala al-thalath

i.e., it nearly exceeded the three. Tha'lab said: no one has said anything better regarding "fa-awla" than what al-Asma'i said. Al-Mubarrad said: it is said to one who intended ruin and then escaped: "awla laka," i.e., you came near to ruin. It is narrated that a Bedouin used to repeatedly shoot at game and miss it, saying "awla laka." Then he shot at an animal, came close to it, then it escaped from him, and he said:

Fa-law kana awla yut'imu al-qawma sidtuhum... wa-lakinna awla yatruku al-qawma juww'a

It was said: it is like a man saying to his companion, "O deprived one, what has escaped you!" Al-Jurjani said: it is derived from "wayl" (woe), so it is af'al, but with inversion (qalb), in that the middle radical of the verb took the place of the lam. The discussion of His saying "fa-awla lahum" is complete. Qatadah said: it is as if He said, "The punishment is nearer to them." It was also said: "wa-liyahumu al-makruh" (disliked things befall them). Then He said: ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾, i.e., obedience and fair speech are better and more fitting. This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil. It was also said: the sense is "amruna ta'atun wa-qawlun ma'ruf" (our matter is obedience and fair speech), with the subject omitted, so one stops at "fa-awla lahum." Likewise for one who estimates "yaqulun minna ta'atan" (they say: from us, obedience). It was also said: the second verse is connected to the first, and the "lam" in His saying "lahum" is in the sense of "ba'" (with/for), i.e., obedience is more fitting and suitable for them and more deserving of them than neglecting the execution of God's command. This is the recitation of Ubayy: "yaqulun ta'atun." It was also said: "ta'atun" is an attribute of "surah," with the sense "fa-idha unzilat surah dhat ta'atin" (when a surah possessing obedience is sent down), so one does not stop at "fa-awla lahum" in this case. Ibn 'Abbas said: their saying "ta'atun" is a report from God, may He be mighty and majestic, about the hypocrites. The meaning is: for them is obedience and fair speech. It was said: it refers to the obligation of the obligatory duties upon them; when the obligations are sent down, their descent is hard for them. Accordingly, one stops here at "fa-awla."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But when the matter is resolved upon﴾, i.e., fighting became serious, or the obligation of fighting became binding, they disliked it. "They disliked it" is the response to "fa-idha," and it is omitted. It was also said: the meaning is "fa-idha 'azama ashab al-amr" (when the people of the matter resolve). ﴿Then if they had been true to God﴾, i.e., in faith and jihad, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾ than disobedience and opposition.

There are four issues here.

**The first issue: his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then is it likely that if you turn away you will cause corruption in the land﴾.** Scholars differed over the meaning of "if you turn away" (in Arabic, *in tawallaytum*). It was said that it derives from *al-wilayah* (authority). Abu al-'Aliyah said: the meaning is, "Would you then be likely, if you were given authority to rule and became rulers, to corrupt the land by taking bribes?" Al-Kalbi said: that is, "Would you then be likely, if you took charge of the affairs of the community, to corrupt the land through injustice?" Ibn Juraij said: the meaning is, "Would you then be likely, if you turned away from obedience, to corrupt the land through sins and by severing the ties of kinship?" Ka'b said: the meaning is, "Would you then be likely, if you took charge of the matter, that some of you would kill others?" It was also said that it derives from *al-i'rad 'an al-shay'* (turning away from something). Qatadah said: that is, "Would you then be likely, if you turned away from the Book of Allah, to corrupt the land by shedding forbidden blood and severing your ties of kinship?" It was also said: "Then is it likely that..." means "Perhaps you, if you turn away from the Qur'an and abandon its rulings, will corrupt the land and return to your former ignorance."

It is also read with *fath* and *kasr* on the sin (*fa-hal 'asaytum* and *fa-hal 'asaytum*). The discussion of this was already given in full in *al-Baqarah* [Cf. vol. 3, p. 244].

Bakr al-Muzani said: it was revealed concerning the Harurites and the Kharijites (an early sect that rebelled against 'Ali and rejected the authority of the community), but this is far-fetched. The more evident view is that it refers to the hypocrites. Ibn Hayyan said: it refers to the Quraysh. Al-Musayyib ibn Sharik and al-Farra' said something similar; they said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Umayyah and the Banu Hashim. The evidence for this interpretation is what 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal narrated, saying: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: ﴿Then is it likely that if you turn away you will cause corruption in the land﴾" — then he said: "They are this clan of the Quraysh. Allah took a covenant from them that, if they ruled the people, they would not cause corruption in the land nor sever their ties of kinship."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib read: "in tuwuliytum an tufsidu fi al-ardh" with a *damma* on the *ta'* and the *waw*, and a *kasra* on the *lam*. This is also the reading of Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Ruways narrated it from Ya'qub. The meaning: "If unjust rulers govern you, you will join them in the strife and fight against them." "And sever your ties of kinship" means by rebellion, injustice and killing.

Ya'qub, Sallam, 'Isa and Abu Hatim read "wa-tuqatti'u" with a *fath* on the *ta'* and a light *qaf*, from *al-qat'*, taking as evidence his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 27]. Harun narrated this reading from Abu 'Amr. Al-Hasan read "wa-tuqatti'u" with all letters vowelled with *fath* and the *ta'* doubled, taking as evidence his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And they divided their affair among themselves﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 93]. The rest read "wa-tuqatti'u" with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a doubled *ta'* (on the *qaf*), from *al-taqti'* (intensive cutting), and this is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd.

The word ﴿'asaytum﴾ was already mentioned in *al-Baqarah* [Al-Baqarah: 246] [Cf. vol. 1, p. 246 and vol. 3, p. 244]. Al-Zajjaj said concerning the reading of Nafi': "If this were permissible, then *'asiya* with *kasra* would also be permissible." Al-Jawhari said: it is said *'asaytu an af'ala dhalika* and *'asiytu* with *kasra*. It was read as "fa-hal 'asiytum" with *kasra*. I say: this statement of his indicates that they are two dialects. The discussion of it was already given in full in *al-Baqarah* [Cf. vol. 1, p. 246 and vol. 3, p. 244].

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾ — that is, He expelled them and removed them far from His mercy. ﴿And has made them deaf﴾ — to the truth. ﴿And blinded their eyes﴾ — that is, their hearts, from good. Thus He followed the report with the statement that whoever does this, his curse is due upon him, and He strips him of the benefit of his hearing and sight, so that he does not submit to the truth even if he hears it, and He makes him like the beast that does not understand. He said, "Then is it likely..." and then said, "Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed," shifting from address to the third person, according to the Arab custom in this.

**The second issue: his saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾** That is, do they not understand it, so that they would know what Allah has prepared for those who did not turn away from Islam? ﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ That is, rather, there are locks upon their hearts which Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, has locked upon them, so they do not understand. This refutes the doctrine of the Qadariyya (who held that human beings create their own actions) and the Imamiyya (the Shi'a who hold to the Imams). In a raised (*marfu'*) hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, upon them are locks like the locks of iron, until Allah opens them."

The root meaning of *al-qafl* is dryness and hardness. It is said of what has dried of plants: *al-qafl*, and *al-qafil* is similar to it. *Al-qafil* is also a plant, and *al-qafil* is also a sound. The reciter (*al-rajiz*) said:

*"When it came to you dry, a withered old man (qirshabba), you stood up to it with the qafil, striking it,*
*how did you lead your old shaykh, the very hairy one?"*

[Cf. vol. 3, p. 4 (244); *al-azabb* (with *fath* and doubled *zay*) means very hairy.] *Al-qirshabb* (with *kasra* on the *qaf*) means the aged, according to al-Asma'i. And *aqfalahu al-sawm* means fasting dried him, according to al-Qushayri and al-Jawhari. So the locks here are an indication of the closing of the heart and its emptiness of faith, meaning that faith does not enter their hearts and unbelief does not leave them, because Allah, may He be exalted, sealed their hearts. He said "upon hearts" because if He had said "upon their hearts," the hearts of others would not be included in this sentence. The intended meaning is: "Or upon the hearts of these people, and the hearts of those who have this attribute, are locks."

**The third issue: in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah created the creation, until when He had finished with them, the womb (*al-rahim*) stood up and said, 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge from severing.' He said: 'Yes. Are you not pleased that I join whoever joins you, and sever whoever severs you?' It said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then that is yours.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿Then is it likely that if you turn away you will cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship? Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, and made them deaf and blinded their eyes. Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾"

The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is an address to all the disbelievers. Qatadah and others said: the meaning of the verse is "perhaps you," or "it is feared for you," if you turn away from faith, that you will return to corruption in the land by shedding blood. Qatadah said: "How did you see the people when they turned away from the Book of Allah, may He be exalted? Did they not shed forbidden blood, sever the ties of kinship and disobey the Merciful?" So the womb according to this is the womb of the religion of Islam and faith, which Allah has named as brotherhood in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 10].

According to the view of al-Farra' that the verse was revealed concerning the Banu Hashim and the Banu Umayyah, what is meant is those among them who concealed hypocrisy. He referred by "severing the ties of kinship" to the kinship that existed between them and the Prophet (ﷺ), by their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ). And that requires fighting.

In sum, the womb (*rahim*) is of two kinds: general and specific. The general is the womb of religion, and it is obligatory to maintain it by holding fast to faith, loving its people, supporting them, giving them sincere counsel, refraining from harming them, being just among them, being fair in dealing with them, and fulfilling their obligatory rights, such as visiting the sick, the rights of the dead including washing them, praying over them and burying them, and other rights due to them. As for the specific womb, which is the womb of kinship from the two sides of a man, his father and his mother, the specific rights are obligatory for them, and more besides, such as providing maintenance, looking after their conditions, and not neglecting to attend to them in times of their need. The general rights of the womb are reinforced in their regard, so that when rights conflict, one begins with the nearest, then the next nearest.

Some scholars said: the womb whose maintenance is obligatory is every womb of a *mahram* (a relative one may not marry), and according to this view, it is not obligatory toward the children of paternal and maternal uncles. It was said: rather, this applies to every womb of those to whom the term applies among the relatives (*dhawu al-arham*) in matters of inheritance, whether a *mahram* or not. From this it follows that the womb of the mother, through which one does not inherit, is not obligatory to maintain, and severing them is not forbidden. This is not correct. The correct view is that everything that the womb includes and embraces must be maintained in every case, as a form of drawing near to Allah and a religious duty, according to what we mentioned first. And Allah knows best.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated in his *Musnad*, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar informed me, saying: I heard Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi narrating from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the womb has a tongue on the Day of Resurrection, beneath the Throne, saying: 'O Lord, I have been severed! O Lord, I have been wronged! O Lord, I have been harmed!' So its Lord answers it: 'Are you not pleased that I join whoever joins you, and sever whoever severs you?'"

In Sahih Muslim, from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The one who severs (the ties of kinship) will not enter Paradise." Ibn Abi 'Umar said: Sufyan said: that is, one who severs the womb. And al-Bukhari narrated it.

**The fourth issue: his saying, peace be upon him: "Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, created the creation, until when He had finished with them..."** "Created" (*khalaqa*) means "brought into being," and its root meaning is measuring, as has already been mentioned [Cf. vol. 1, p. 226]. And "the creation" (*al-khalq*) here means the created thing. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqman: 11], meaning His creature. And the meaning of "finished with them" is: He perfected their creation, not that He was occupied with them and then finished with His occupation with them, since His action is not by direct contact or by handling, nor is His creating by an instrument or by effort, exalted is He above that. And His saying, "The womb stood up and said," is to be understood in one of two ways. The first: that Allah, may He be exalted, appointed one of the angels to speak on behalf of the womb and to say this, as if He had entrusted this worship to one who would defend it, and would record the reward of the one who maintained it and the burden of the one who severed it, just as Allah entrusted all other deeds to the noble recording angels, and to the angels who succeed one another by witnessing the times of the prayers. The second: that this is by way of depiction and illustration, conveying exhaustion and the intensity of concern. So it is as if He said: "If the womb were one who understands and speaks, it would say these words," just as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of Allah﴾, then He said: ﴿And those are the parables We set forth for the people, that perhaps they will reflect﴾ [Al-Hashr: 21].

His saying, "It said: 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge with You from severing,'" the purpose of this statement is to inform of the emphasis upon the matter of maintaining the ties of kinship, and that Allah, glory be to Him, has placed it in the position of one who seeks protection from Him and whom He grants protection, and admits him into His covenant and His protection.

And since this is so, the protection of Allah is not forsaken, and His covenant is not broken. For this reason He said, addressing the womb: "Are you not pleased that I join whoever joins you, and sever whoever severs you?" This is like his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever prays the dawn prayer is in the protection of Allah, the Exalted, so let Allah not demand anything from you of His protection, for whoever is demanded anything of His protection, He will overtake him and then throw him face down into the Fire."

Allah's words: ﴿So how will it be﴾, meaning, how will their condition be? The meaning of the statement is warning and threat: that is, if the punishment is delayed for them, then it will come by the end of their lifetimes. That is, that is their recompense. "Because they followed what displeased Allah" (ittaba'u ma askhata Allah). It was also said: their grudges. Its singular is dhighn. The poet said:

"And one with spite whom I restrained myself from"

This has already been mentioned. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"Spite after spite spreads over you,
and brings out the hidden disease."

"As if he were carrying a child under his arm"

That is, carrying him in his lap. Ibn Muqbil said:

"When I carry my weapon beside its flank,
and an elbow like the hilt of a sword when dried up."

One morning they awoke and on the forehead of each one of them was written: "This is a hypocrite." That was their mark.

Ibn Zayd said: Allah decreed their exposure and ordered that they be expelled from the mosque, but they refused except to hold fast to "There is no god but Allah." Thus their blood was protected, and they married and were married through it.

"And you will surely know them by the tone of their speech" – that is, by its implication and meaning. From this is the poet's saying:

"The best speech is that which is allusive (lahn)."

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "You bring your disputes before me, and perhaps some of you is more eloquent (alhan) in his argument than another," meaning he is more able to carry it in reply, being stronger in turning speech.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 47, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely test you﴾, meaning, We will make you worship through the sharia (the revealed laws), even though We already know the outcomes of matters. It was also said: We will deal with you as those who are being tested. "Until We know those among you who strive and are patient" in it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Until We know" means until We distinguish. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Until We know" means until We see. This has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 156, second edition.]]. The recitation of the majority is with the nun in "la-nabluwannakum" and "na'lama" and "wa-nabluwa". Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read with the ya' in all of them. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, related the sukun on the waw of "nabluw" as a resumption (qat') from what precedes it. The rest read it in the accusative (nasb), as a response (radd) to His saying: "until We know" (hatta na'lama). This knowledge is the knowledge by which the recompense occurs, because He only recompenses them for their deeds, not for His eternal knowledge of them. So its interpretation is: until We know the strivers with knowledge of witnessing (ilm shahadah), because when they are commanded to act, what they do is witnessed from them, so the recompense of reward and punishment falls upon the knowledge of witnessing. "And We will test your reports" (wa-nabluwa akhbarakum): We will examine them and make them manifest. Ibrahim ibn al-Ash'ath said: Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, whenever he recited this verse, would weep and say: "O Allah, do not test us, for if You test us You will expose us and tear away our veils."

"It refers to the hypocrites, or to the Jews." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They are those who fed (the polytheists) on the day of Badr." Its parallel is ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 36], and so on [[Verse 36 of Surat al-Anfal.]]. "And opposed the Messenger" means they were hostile to him and went against him. "After guidance had become clear to them" means they knew that he was a prophet through the proofs and signs. "They will not harm Allah at all" by their disbelief. "And He will nullify their deeds" means the reward for what they had done.

**First issue:** Allah's words: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾. When He had described the state of the disbelievers, He commanded the believers to hold fast to obedience in His commands and to the Messenger's ordinances (sunan).

"And do not invalidate your deeds" (﴿وَلا تُبْطِلُوا أَعْمالَكُمْ﴾), meaning your good deeds, by acts of disobedience. This is the view of al-Hasan. Al-Zuhri said: by major sins (al-kaba'ir). Ibn Jurayj said: by showing off (riya') and seeking reputation (sum'ah).

Muqatil and al-Thumali said: by reminding others of favours (al-mann), and this address was to those who used to remind the Prophet (ﷺ) of their having embraced Islam. All of these are close in meaning, and al-Hasan's statement encompasses them. The verse also indicates that major sins invalidate acts of worship, and that acts of disobedience take a person out of faith.

**Second issue:** Our scholars and others have cited this verse as evidence that breaking off a voluntary act (tatawwu') after one has begun it, whether prayer or fasting, is not permissible, because it involves invalidating the deed, which Allah has forbidden.

Those who permitted it, among them Imam al-Shafi'i and others, said: the intended meaning is the invalidation of the reward of an obligatory act, so the person is forbidden from nullifying its reward. As for what is voluntary (nafl), it does not fall under this, because it is not obligatory upon him. If they claim that the wording is general, then a general statement may be specified. The basis for specifying it is that the nafl is a voluntary act (tatawwu'), and voluntariness implies choice.

Abu al-'Aliyah reported that they used to hold that no sin harms a person who is a Muslim, until this verse was revealed, and then they feared that major sins would invalidate their deeds.

Muqatil said: Allah the Exalted says, "If you disobey the Messenger, you have invalidated your deeds."

He explains that the consideration (of the verse) is that dying in disbelief necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire. The discussion of this has already passed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 3, p. (48)]]. It has also been said that the verse refers to the people of the well [[The well of Badr is meant.]], and its ruling is general.

The first issue concerns the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So do not weaken﴾, meaning do not become feeble in fighting. *Al-wahn* means weakness. One says *wahana al-insan* and *wahanahu ghayruh*, and the verb is used both transitively and intransitively. The poet said:

*"Indeed, I am not one who can be made weak by poverty"*

[This is the second half of a verse by Tarafa, whose first half is: *"And when you sting me, I sting back."*]

*Wahna* (with a kasra on the ha) also means weakness. It is read as *fa-ma wahanu* with a damma and with a kasra on the ha. This has been discussed in (Al ʿImran) [see vol. 4, p. 230].

The second issue concerns the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and call to peace﴾, meaning reconciliation. "And you are the superior ones" means that you are more knowledgeable of Allah than they are. It has also been said: "And you are the superior ones" in argument. It has also been said: the meaning is "and you are the victorious ones," because you are believers, even if they overcome you outwardly in some circumstances. Qatada said: "Do not be the first of the two groups to humble itself before its companion."

The third issue: the scholars differed about its ruling. It has been said that it abrogates (*naskh*) the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [Al-Anfal: 61], because Allah the Exalted forbade inclining toward reconciliation when the Muslims had no need of it. It has also been said that it is abrogated by the words of Allah the Exalted: "And if they incline to peace, then incline to it." It has also been said that it is *muhkam* (not abrogated). The two verses were revealed at two different times with different circumstances. It has also been said that the words "And if they incline to peace, then incline to it" are specific to particular people, while the other verse is general. Therefore, a truce with the disbelievers is not permitted except in cases of necessity, namely when we are unable to resist them because the Muslims are weak. This meaning has already been discussed fully [see vol. 8, p. 69].

﴿And Allah is with you﴾, meaning with help and support, like the words: ﴿And indeed Allah is with the doers of good﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 69].

﴿And He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾, meaning He will not diminish them for you. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others. From the same root comes *al-mawtur*, the one whose slain relative has not been avenged, so his blood-debt remains unrequited. One says *watarahu yatiruhu, witran, wa-tiratan*. From the same root is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, it is as if he has lost his family and his property," meaning that he has been robbed of them. Similarly, *watarahu haqqahu* means he diminished his right.

Allah the Exalted's words ﴿and He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾ mean He will not reduce your deeds. As one says, "I entered the house," meaning "into the house," as al-Jawhari said. Al-Farra' said: "*Lan yatirakum*" is derived from *al-watr*, which means "the single," so the meaning is: "He will not leave you single (or alone) without reward."

Abu Ma'mar from 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr read "wa-yukhriju" with a raised ya' on the jim, as an inceptive, resumptive construction.
